claims.text: Bulk-like sluggish diffusion breaks down in Au-Co-Cu-Ni-Pt nanoparticles below a critical diameter of approximately 5 nm.
The breakdown of sluggish diffusion is caused by surface-energy minimization and rapid surface-mediated segregation.
Surface-mediated segregation produces Ostwald ripening and particle-shape anisotropy rather than thermodynamic stabilization.
The initial nanoparticles are equiatomic Au-Co-Cu-Ni-Pt with a uniform elemental distribution.
Carbothermal shock or a similar nonequilibrium method can synthesize uniformly mixed, sub-10 nm nanoparticles containing the target elements.
A vacuum pressure below 10^-6 Pa removes oxidative interference during heating.
The nanoparticle surface-to-volume ratio scales inversely with particle radius.
Surface diffusion coefficients scale inversely with particle radius.
At sufficiently small particle sizes, surface diffusion overrides bulk lattice-diffusion barriers.
During heating, Au preferentially migrates to the surface or coalesces.
During heating, Co and Ni preferentially segregate to the core or form distinct phases.
In these nanoparticles, the energetic drive to reduce surface energy exceeds stabilization from entropy of mixing.
Particles smaller than 5 nm disappear through Ostwald ripening, transferring mass to larger particles.
The surviving particles develop faceting, nonspherical shapes, or core-shell structures indicative of elemental segregation.
Bulk HEA theory predicts that high entropy and sluggish diffusion maintain a single-phase, spherical structure stable up to 1000 K.
For bulk alloys or particles larger than 20 nm, sluggish diffusion prevents rapid phase separation.
The critical size at which surface effects overtake entropy stabilization depends on the alloy's mixing enthalpies.
